articles.title: Gloria Steinem Was the Godmother of Neoliberal Feminism
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content: Gloria Steinem, the establishment’s favorite radical feminist, died on September 2. The mainstream media has gone all out in praising her, with the Wall Street Journal and The New York Times united in their adulation. The Times called her the “personification of the women’s movement” and credited her with helping to usher in “sweeping cultural transformations across virtually every facet of American life, from the boardroom to the courtroom to the bedroom.” They approvingly quote her self-description as an “entrepreneur of social change.” For many people, she is the only radical feminist they can name, eclipsing the extraordinary women who planned and launched the successful women’s liberation movement starting in 1967. Steinem did wield enormous influence. Ms . magazine and the Ms. Foundation for Women, which she cofounded, came to define what was worthy in the feminist project. But to the women’s liberation pioneers she displaced, this meant silencing the radicals and promoting the anodyne. When Steinem described Ms . as “a kind of connective tissue for women all across this country who felt isolated until we came along and let them know they were not alone,” feminist pioneers saw Steinem as taking credit for work already done by the movement. The women’s liberation movement didn’t need Ms . to publicize it. It had already been on the front page of nearly every mass circulation magazine and had produced ten mass-market anthologies by 1971, selling millions of copies. The movement published one hundred small newspapers and journals, including Off Our Backs , It Ain’t Me Babe , and Woman’s World . And it had already won substantial victories by the time Steinem emerged on the scene. Thousands of working-class women were suing employers for sex discrimination. Abortion was legalized in New York State in 1970. The Equal Rights Amendment passed the House of Representatives in 1971 and the Senate in March 1972, followed immediately by twenty-two states. The Rise of Ms. Magazine So it was with an eye to the market already created by the radicals that Steinem, then thirty-seven and a professional magazine writer, collaborated with New York magazine editor Clay Felker to start Ms . magazine. The inaugural issue appeared as a section of New York in December 1971; it launched separately in July 1972. Washington Post publisher Katharine Graham invested, and Warner Communications put in $1 million but asked only for a 25 percent stake, an unusually generous arrangement. Some women’s liberation pioneers were at first glad to hear of the new publication. Kathie Sarachild of Redstockings , who coined the phrase “Sisterhood Is Powerful” and authored the germinal 1968 “Program for Feminist Consciousness-Raising,” said she initially though Ms . would act as a feminist muckraker magazine, doing investigative journalism on behalf of women’s cause. She and other women’s liberation movement founders were soon disillusioned. It’s not that Steinem didn’t know who had led the movement up to the point she entered. In 1969, writing for New York magazine, she had attended the first-ever Redstockings abortion speak-out. She recalled the scene in her 1983 book, Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions : A local feminist group had asked women to testify about their real life experiences with illegal abortion. I sat in a church basement listening to women stand before an audience and talk about desperately trying to find someone who would help them, enduring pre-abortion rapes from doctors, being asked to accept sterilization as the price of abortion, and endangering their lives in an illegal, unsafe medical underground. . . . Suddenly I was no longer learning intellectually what was wrong. I knew. I had had an abortion when I was newly out of college, and had told no one. Yet the women who had taught her so much largely failed to find a place in the pages of Ms . three years later. Ellen Willis, pop music critic for The New Yorker and a Redstockings founder, did manage to make the cut starting in 1973. She resigned after two years, calling Ms . editorial policy “conservative, anti-left feminism.” In her resignation letter, Willis wrote: “No attempt has ever been made to recruit and hire experienced feminist writers, theorists, organizers. . . . Ms .’s politics [include] a mushy, sentimental idea of sisterhood designed to obscure political conflicts between women.” “Basically, it’s a change yourself line, the women’s magazine line,” Sarachild reflected later. “But the tricky thing about Ms . is that they pretend to be different. I bet there are certain women who wouldn’t bother reading women’s magazines who read Ms .” The editing reflected the politics, and radicals described Ms . editing as torture. Patricia Mainardi, author of the groundbreaking 1968 manifesto the “The Politics of Housework,” recalled: They would use a bullshit word instead of a strong word. I had the word “loved.” They changed it to “had a fondness for.” . . . Cindy Nemser wrote in an article about Alice Neel, “Alice Neel is the foremost portrait painter in our time.” In Ms . this became, “She may indeed be the foremost portrait painter of the last 40 years.” It’s sneaky editing, downgrading women’s contribution to art. Ms .’s line is women are no good in art. They have been oppressed and damaged by their oppression. They’re inferior. It’s a goody-goody line: we have to work harder to overcome our oppression. This made a sad contrast to the radicals, whose daring truth-telling had organized millions on the idea that what appeared to be women’s individual, personal problems were in fact political and rooted in their oppression by men. This was what they meant by the slogan “ The Personal Is Political .” Establishment Feminism Ms . pioneered the use of private foundation funding to steer feminist movement priorities. The Ms. Foundation dispensed money to approved feminist projects and created a database of feminists around the country and the world. It seeded the founding of the National Black Feminist Organization (NBFO), a Ms .-aligned black women’s group. The NBFO is often cited as the very first black feminist organization in the United States. Repeating the pattern for the women’s liberation movement as a whole, the group blotted out the more radical organizing that preceded it, including the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee Black Women’s Liberation Committee, its successor, the Third World Women’s Alliance, and the Patricia Robinson–led group Poor Black Women, all groups with radical and anti-imperialist politics. Before the rise of Ms ., movement originators had received widespread coverage. Kate Millett was on the cover of Time in 1970. That same year hundreds of feminists occupied the offices of Ladies’ Home Journal editor John Mack Carter, demanding an issue they edited (and free daycare for the magazine’s workforce). They won an eight-page supplement titled “The New Feminism.” But soon, the media went to Steinem for their “radical” feminism. Redstockings called it the “historic invisibility treatment”: The women who developed the movement’s strategy were written out of the picture. They became anonymous foremothers — while many were still in their twenties and thirties. Betty Friedan was too well-known to sideline, but the media loved to counterpose Steinem to Friedan, the older, unhip, allegedly less radical feminist who founded the National Organization for Women in 1966. In fact, Friedan’s politics were well to the left of Steinem’s — under her maiden name, Goldstein, Friedan had served as a staffer of the United Electrical, Radio and Machine Workers of America, the union that held out against the demand that US unions expel their leftist leaders. While Friedan presented herself as reformist to evade red-baiting, she argued astutely for undermining the the basis of men’s power over women by advocating for programs and structures that would give women the economic foundation for independence from men. “Without childcare, it’s all just talk,” she argued. Steinem, styled as more radical, volunteered for Angela Davis’s bail committee, posed with her fist raised with Dorothy Pittman Hughes in October 1971, and toured the country with radical black lawyer Florynce Kennedy to lecture on feminism. Steinem loved witty aphorisms that expressed terrible politics. She quoted actress Lee Grant: “I’ve been married to a Marxist and a Fascist, and neither one of them ever took out the garbage.” Aside from garbage being a rare bit of male-coded housework, the quote implies that communists and fascists are equally bad. You wouldn’t expect a fascist to do housework. She liked to quote a woman cab driver in Boston who told her, “If men could get pregnant, abortion would be a sacrament.” While funny, this gets the causality of women’s oppression backward. Founding radical feminist theorist Simone de Beauvoir argued that women are oppressed because we do reproductive labor: if men could get pregnant, they would be the oppressed sex. Steinem’s concept of a “liberated woman” (who, as she quipped, has sex before marriage and a job after) directly contradicted the the very heart of the radical movement’s argument — that women are oppressed as a class and can’t make themselves free individually. Where did her politics come from? She seemed have one foot in the establishment from the start, dating John F. Kennedy speechwriter Ted Sorensen; then Franklin Thomas, who would soon lead the Ford Foundation; and, in the 1980s, real estate developer Mortimer Zuckerman. Vivian Gornick recalled, “Gloria was uptown; we were downtown. She hung out with Establishment figures; we had only ourselves.” Steinem and the CIA In 1967, the left-wing magazine Ramparts exposed the river of secret CIA money flowing into the National Student Association, the United States’ largest student group. After the revelations, Steinem spoke to the press about her role in recruiting anti-communist students to attend and disrupt the World Youth Festivals, which started in the socialist world and planned for the first time to venture outside the iron curtain in Vienna in 1959 and Helsinki in 1962. She worked full-time as director of the Independent Service for Information on the Vienna Youth Festival, later renamed the Independent Research Service (IRS), a CIA conduit that flooded the festivals with anti-communist and pro-US propaganda. At the Helsinki festival, which drew 18,000 people from 137 countries, the IRS produced a daily newspaper published in three languages, coedited by Steinem and Clay Felker. One of the 1959 publications with her name on it, A Review of Negro Segregation in the United States , claimed that the problem of racial discrimination had essentially been solved in the United States and that leftover problems were due to black people’s psychology. Low voter registration was because “in many areas of the South there exists a profound apathy among Negroes to the this paramount responsibility of good citizenship.” The CIA’s goal had been to make the festivals so fraught — by encouraging violent clashes — that the countries sponsoring them would cancel them. As it turned out, the following two were canceled because the planned hosts, Algeria in 1965 and then Ghana in 1966, experienced coups. In Ghana, the CIA was involved, according to agency officer John Stockwell. In the 1967 interviews, Steinem said the CIA funding was no problem. “Far from being shocked by this involvement I was happy to find some liberals in government in those days who were far-sighted and cared enough to get Americans of all political views to the festival,” she told The New York Times . She also said she was not asked to report on people she met there. Since Steinem wasn’t well-known at the time, it was eight years later that the New York–based feminist group Redstockings discovered the connection, after Steinem had rocketed to the front of the movement. Redstockings published an exposé in 1975, suggesting that the substitution of Ms . and Steinem for the “original, authentic activists that started the movement” looked similar to other CIA operations that “create or support ‘parallel’ organizations which provide an alternative to radicalism.” It also pointed out that a report published by Steinem’s organization on the Vienna festival included short dossiers on dozens of student leaders from around the world — contrary to her claim she never reported on attendees. Steinem at first refused to respond to the charges, but when she did, she again defended her role and that of the CIA at the festivals. However, she did put considerable effort into suppressing the argument made by Redstockings. Random House planned to bring out a mass-market edition of the self-published book Redstockings book Feminist Revolution , which included a chapter on Steinem. Steinem threatened to sue Random House, and the publisher caved and censored the chapter. Steinem’s lawyers also threatened The Village Voice and even sent a threatening letter to every member of the board of the Columbia Tenants Union in New York City when its newspaper, The Heights and Valley News , printed a series on Steinem and the censorship. Women’s Equality and the Neoliberal Turn By the late 1980s, Steinem was famous for Ms . and for being the radical feminist but had not yet written a book laying out her vision of feminism (the anthology Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions in 1983 collected her writing in Ms .and elsewhere). When it finally came, Revolution From Within: A Book of Self-Esteem (1992) affirmed everything about her politics that had dismayed the radicals who started the movement. The book, which received a six-figure advance, continued the women’s magazine line that women needed to make internal changes. “Without self-esteem, the only change is an exchange of masters; with it, there is no need for masters,” she wrote. Of course, we don’t have masters because we need them but because they need us . This basic inversion was symptomatic of her politics. By contrast, women’s liberation feminists argued that women, like other oppressed people, are in constant struggle against our bonds — a concept they called the “Pro-Woman Line” — in fact, we take every bit of space available and find ingenious workarounds even when there is none. It was discrimination, exploitation, punishment, and constant everyday pressure that constrained us. This hard-won analysis was developed through the main program of the movement, consciousness-raising . Ms . watered down this important organizing tool, publishing a guide to consciousness-raising that used the name and the form but missed the substance, reducing it to a therapy group where women blew off steam and got sisterly support. The original idea was to use the data that emerged in testimony to assess women’s true situation, dig at the root cause, and analyze who benefits. The program was inspired by the Southern civil rights movement’s “tell it like it is” public testifying and had parallels in the Chinese Revolution’s “speak bitterness” sessions. It was not intended as a safe space. As corporate attacks in the late 1970s and early ’80s destroyed unions and working-class living conditions and wages plunged for all workers, Friedan and feminist radicals alike argued that advancing women’s equality now required confrontation with corporate power to get guarantees of childcare and health care, paid family leave, and shorter work hours for everyone. Friedan called it the “second stage” of feminism in a book by that name. Redstockings called for the abolition of private health insurance companies and a robust social wage, to give women independence from men and employers. The Ms . wing of the movement fragmented into thousands of nonprofits, competing for grants from rich people by each proposing “winnable” small-bore solutions to the wreckage left by the employer offensive. This blinkered feminist vision was reflected in the Democratic Party establishment. Meanwhile, long hours, low pay, and worsening conditions for raising kids made women vulnerable to a right-wing nostalgia for to the “glorious thirty” postwar years of family-supporting jobs and stay-at-home moms. In recent years, Steinem dropped all pretense of radicalism. She supported Hillary Clinton in the 2016 Democratic primary against Bernie Sanders, and in an interview that year on Real Time With will Maher suggested that young women only supported Sanders because “that’s where the boys are; the boys are with Bernie.” She later claimed she misspoke. Media hagiography of Steinem reached a fever pitch in the last decade with a TV dramatization of her life, The Glorias ; a play, Gloria: A Life ; and glowing profiles in the The New York Times , The New Yorker , and elsewhere. This wave of Steinem-mania coincided with a time that young women were questioning the utility of a 1 percent feminism, represented by such figures as Clinton, Madeleine Albright , and Sheryl Sandberg . Had the goal of women’s liberation really been exploitative corporations and a violent US empire run by women? Steinem was again trotted out to steer the discussion into safe channels, but by the time of her appearance with Maher, she was just giving feminists a bad name. Women’s liberation movement pioneers, to a woman, came out of the civil rights movement, the antiwar movement, and the student left. They believed that consistent feminism leads to socialism, and vice versa. Following Beauvoir, they wanted to dig deep and abolish the exploitation of women and the oppression required to maintain it. Starting in the 1960s, they planned and built a successful radical movement that profoundly changed the situation of women in the United States and reverberated worldwide. It’s a crime that their movement was for fifty years personified by someone who never shared its goals.

articles.title: Organizing from the Bottom: IBEW’s Fight for Sanitary Facilities
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content: Workers in high-visibility gear gather at a downtown Detroit worksite, with the city skyline visible in the background. By Kevin Szczesny To get clean Porta-johns in our workplace, construction workers at the Marriott site in downtown Detroit marched on the boss. Workers from at least seven unions of the building trades were represented, with zero union staffers or officers present. Many union halls were in support of the action, but the work and the application of leverage were entirely rank-and-file driven. As an active member of IBEW Local 58 (Electrical Workers), I often hear from sympathetic organizers who “can’t imagine how hard it must be” organizing in a largely conservative and obstinate workforce. Our campaign is a contribution to the death of that narrative, and an answer to the universal follow-up question about how these shop floor conversations go in detail. Day One on the job, as I met my 50 or so fellow electricians, I was immediately overwhelmed with warnings that the bathrooms were going to be unsanitary. I knew before the end of my shift that the issue was widely felt, and every electrician already had the same idea: we wanted the cleaning schedule changed from twice a week to three times a week. I had a long conversation with the steward about what efforts were already in progress to correct the issue. The first instinct of a construction worker is to “drag” (quit), drive over to the union hall, and pick up a new job. As expected, there was a steady trickle of drags and conditions on site had not improved. OSHA had been called and walked the job soon after my arrival, only to say that the number of bathrooms was up to their standard. The electrical contractor had been notified, but because the bathrooms were for all of the trades to use, our bosses didn’t feel it was their responsibility to pay for additional cleaning. The local IBEW contract only gestures vaguely to “sanitary facilities,” and protects us explicitly should we leave site to find a “sanitary” facility. This clause was exercised regularly, but no one could say for sure whether the boss was even aware we were leaving. Over time, smaller issues would pop up and get resolved quickly with small actions. Sweeping compound to control toxic dust, unprecedented changes in break time, trades doing the work of other trades out of convenience: these were things that were easily managed by the steward with one or two voices in support. I got involved with a couple pushes and so was asked to fill in for the steward while he was out for a few days. When I walked the job to make sure everyone had my number, more than half the conversations touched on the bathrooms. I then introduced myself to the stewards from the other trades, who all encountered the same comments from their members. The idea was formed to take the issue above our bosses and straight to the general contractor (who hires out each trade and is responsible for the job site at large). A letter was written titled “Unacceptable Bathroom Conditions,” which opened politely and assumed the boss was ignorant of the problem. The letter referenced the impact on our work and a widespread feeling that we were not being treated with respect by the contractor. We suggested that the person responsible for scheduling use our bathrooms for a week, to better assess the need for more cleanings and a wash station. We gave one week for a response. Every worker who was presented with the letter signed immediately, but reactions were mixed. Most people felt like they would just laugh at our demand, but were interested in the idea of swarming the bosses’ trailer at lunch and forcing them to read it in front of us.We fielded many suggestions, from delivering the letter and going home to tipping over Porta-johns on the way to the boss, and we told our coworkers that if our response date came and went without change, we would be coming back around “to have a different conversation.” This demand had to be made collectively and clearly first so that any future action would be naturally tied to the lack of clean facilities, and we had to start our escalation low enough that further demonstrations would be felt. Many of our one-on-one talks were focused on assuring the workers that we would circle back for an escalation if the letter went ignored. “This is only the beginning”, “they probably will ignore this or lie, but we need to show that we’re all on the same page first,” “dragging only leaves behind the people who can’t quit with shitty conditions,” etc. We warned of possible counter-strategies from the boss and stressed the importance of demonstrating solidarity, especially across the trades, above all else. We also left out the officers at the hall and our reps on purpose, though we did inform them. We had a lot of conversations about the power in the hands of the rank-and-file. “Every member is a steward” has become sort of a slogan for us. In the end we had 105 signatures and roughly 35 folks across four trades who gave up their lunch break to deliver the letter. The contractor read that letter, was brought outside to look at us, and immediately conceded to our terms. Maybe they didn’t know how bad the bathrooms were, maybe they didn’t know how widely and deeply felt the issue was on site, or maybe they figured it was fine to ignore. All we know for sure is, when a seemingly small fraction of us came together with the backing of three times as many signatures, it didn’t matter if we had the hall behind us. We are the union, the working people who don’t walk away from a job which doesn’t satisfy us, and our demands have been met. Kevin is a trade unionist and has been a member of the IBEW for two years and DSA member for five. Organizing from the Bottom: IBEW’s Fight for Sanitary Facilities was originally published in The Detroit Socialist on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

articles.title: Ruth First’s Legacy Has Outlived the Regime That Killed Her
articles.author: Christopher J. Lee
articles.content: In August 1982, a parcel bomb went off at the Center for African Studies at Eduardo Mondlane University in Maputo, Mozambique. Sent by the South African government’s Special Branch, its target and victim was Ruth First, a lifelong member of the South African Communist Party (SACP), who was fifty-seven years old at the time. Her assassination has since become the stuff of legend, a symbol of the violent brutality of the apartheid government toward its critics in the last decades of its existence. The murder of First was part of a broader effort by the white minority state to eliminate its opponents following the Soweto Uprising of 1976, which resulted in a revival of (and a generational shift within) the anti-apartheid struggle. Inspired by the ideas of Steve Biko, the Black Consciousness Movement took to the streets of townships across South Africa. Facing arrest and often worse, many sought refuge and exile in neighboring countries, the so-called Frontline States, which included Botswana, Tanzania, Zambia, Angola, Zimbabwe, and Mozambique. Counterinsurgency raids by the South African Defense Force and Special Branch units ensued, targeting these activists with little regard for the national sovereignty of the countries where they had taken shelter. Ruth First cut a different profile from many other liberation figures. A generation older than the members of the Black Consciousness Movement, she undermines many stereotypes about who was involved in the struggle, for what reasons, and to what ends. Her assassination underscored the complex and evolutionary nature of South Africa’s liberation history and the extreme lengths that the apartheid government would go to avoid its demise. Beginnings Born in Johannesburg on May 4, 1925, Heloise Ruth First was white, Jewish, middle class, university educated, a wife, and a mother of three daughters. Each of these qualities informed her activism in distinctive ways, positioning her at different moments as a political outsider, a party confidant, a fiercely engaged intellectual, and a mother both protective and absent, depending on the circumstances. Her husband, Joe Slovo, was a key figure in the SACP and one of the founders of uMkhonto weSizwe (MK), the military wing of the African National Congress (ANC) and the SACP that was established in 1961. He later became general secretary of the SACP and minister of housing in South Africa’s post-apartheid government during Nelson Mandela’s presidency. First’s life reflected this personal and political partnership, with her actions and outlook shaped by their marriage, if not always determined by it. Indeed, although the role of the family in liberation struggles has at times been recognized, it has frequently been under-conceptualized as a source of political influence and decision-making, in addition to providing security, comfort, and support during periods of political uncertainty. The patriarchal norms of anti-colonial movements have too often been reproduced uncritically, with the heroes and philosophers of revolution remaining men — think of Frantz Fanon, Patrice Lumumba, and Steve Biko. To guard against this tendency, it is important to grasp how personal networks among families and peers alike contributed to the making of liberation ideals and actions. Alan Wieder has noted in his dual biography of First and Slovo how the anti-apartheid struggle in particular was defined by couples, with Nelson and Winnie Mandela epitomizing such intimate political partnerships. First and Slovo’s marriage was equally emblematic of the intersection between political and private commitments. Ruth First herself grew up in a political household, which shaped her socialist outlook and activist future. Her father, Julius, and mother, Tilly, emigrated to Johannesburg from Latvia and Lithuania, respectively, as part of a broader influx of Jewish immigrants to South Africa during the first decades of the twentieth century. Both became involved with the Communist Party of South Africa (CPSA), as the party was named after its founding in 1921. Ruth First enrolled at the University of the Witwatersrand, where she met Slovo, who had returned to South Africa after having served in World War II. The CPSA had supported the fight against Nazi fascism. She also became friends with Mandela and other student activists like Harold Wolpe, who later became known for pioneering the concept of racial capitalism. First’s student activism soon extended beyond campus through her support of the 1946 miners’ strike, which involved approximately 74,000 Black workers. Following the economic stresses of World War II, it proved to be a pivotal moment in labor organizing, extending a long tradition of industrial action that struck at the heart of the country’s mineral economy and its exploitation of black South Africans. Finding a vocation for journalism, First went on to write for the Guardian in Johannesburg and New Age , a leftist paper aligned with the ANC, where she covered black politics. She and Slovo became romantically involved in 1948, the year the conservative National Party came to power with its extremist platform of racial segregation known as apartheid. They married the following year in 1949. Activism and Repression The 1950s were a heady period of activism and even optimism, when the possibility of toppling the apartheid government seemed within reach. The 1950 Suppression of Communism Act forced the CPSA to dissolve publicly and reform underground as the SACP. This shift converged with a growing alliance between the SACP and the ANC. This partnership had origins going back to the 1920s, when James La Guma of the CPSA and Josiah Tshangana Gumede of the ANC both attended the 1927 League Against Imperialism conference in Brussels. They traveled on to Moscow where together they met with Nikolai Bukharin, then general secretary of the Communist International (Comintern). This meeting resulted in the Native Republic thesis, a two-part political strategy for South Africa that argued for black national liberation in advance of communist revolution. This approach came out of Vladimir Lenin’s “Draft Theses on National and Colonial Questions,” which were issued at the Second Congress of the Communist International in 1920. Though the CPSA had dropped the thesis as an explicit platform by the time of World War II, its general approach informed the ANC-SACP alliance in the decades ahead. For SACP members, the thinking behind the alliance was as follows: the ANC would spearhead a black liberation struggle aimed at achieving a national democratic revolution, which would be succeeded in turn by a SACP-led socialist state. This collaboration generated intellectual debates over the national question and the idea that South Africa constituted a “colonialism of a special type.” Members of both organizations viewed the system of apartheid as fundamentally colonial in nature through its elements of political disenfranchisement and economic extraction, thus aligning their ambitions with anti-colonial movements across Africa and around the world. However, there was less clarity around questions of political timing, tactical coordination, and what a future South Africa might look like. Such questions would preoccupy First in the decades ahead. The defendants at the Treason Trial pose for a photo in December 1956. (Eli Weinberg / Mayibuye Archive) Under the leadership of Chief Albert Luthuli, the ANC spearheaded the multiracial Congress Alliance during the 1950s with mass actions, including the 1952 Defiance Campaign, which involved strikes, boycotts, and civil disobedience against pass laws and other apartheid measures. This public resistance culminated with the Congress of the People in 1955, held in Soweto, which involved the member organizations of the Congress Alliance and resulted in the promulgation of the Freedom Charter, which demanded a nonracial, fully democratic South Africa. The apartheid government responded swiftly by arresting 156 activists for their involvement in the Congress of the People, accusing them of attempting to overthrow the state. First and Slovo were among those detained. The Treason Trial subsequently unfolded from 1956 to 1961, depriving the activists of political momentum but also providing them with a stage to communicate their anti-racist principles to a global audience. The Treason Trial proved to be a moment of public solidarity that unified different activists across organizations, genders, and racial lines. In addition to First and Slovo, among the accused were Nelson Mandela, Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu, Moses Kotane, Helen Joseph, Ahmed Kathrada, and Alex La Guma. Mandela would later quip in his autobiography that the trial was “the largest and longest unbanned meeting of the Congress Alliance in years.” Sharpeville Though all the accused were eventually acquitted, the protracted nature of the Treason Trial created an opening for other parties, principally the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC). Founded by Robert Sobukwe, a former ANC member, the PAC emphasized a more strident black nationalism in contrast to the multiracial front of the Congress Alliance. Sobukwe served as a forerunner to Biko and the Black Consciousness movement of the late 1960s and ’70s. On March 21, 1960, the PAC organized a pass law protest involving an estimated five thousand people in Sharpeville. Police opened fire, killing at least ninety-one people and injuring hundreds more. This proved to be a turning point in the history of the liberation struggle. The apartheid government reacted to the Sharpeville Massacre by declaring a state of emergency and banning the PAC and the ANC. Sharpeville also prompted the turn to armed struggle by the ANC and SACP in 1961. Mandela, Slovo, and First were key figures in the development and implementation of this new strategy, which marked a generational shift away from the civil disobedience approach of Luthuli. The next several decades would be defined by the maneuvers of MK, linking the ANC and the SACP with other liberation struggles in Africa as well as similar movements in Southeast Asia, Latin America, and Palestine. The banning of the ANC and the escalation of police surveillance had a major impact on First’s life. She traveled to Swaziland (present-day Eswatini) with her daughters shortly after the state of emergency was declared, at a time when Slovo was detained. She eventually returned to continue her work as a journalist, though her situation began to unravel in 1962 once Mandela and other activists were arrested for their militant activities. The subsequent Rivonia Trial led to Mandela’s sentence of life imprisonment along with seven others in 1964. First herself was detained in August 1963 after police raided her home and found illicit political material. Slovo had already left South Africa in June for what was intended to be a temporary mission for MK. Incarcerated under the ninety-day detention law, First ultimately spent 117 days in prison, an experience retold in her memoir, 117 Days (1965), which conveyed the inhumanity of the apartheid regime for a global audience. “Left in that cell long enough, I feared to become one of those colourless insects that slither under a world of flat, grey stones, away from the sky and the sunlight, the grass and people,” First wrote, depicting the escalating sense of dehumanization she felt. Yet 117 Days also describes her resistance to this process, with the prison symbolizing the broader apparatus of the apartheid state through the cruel spatial intimacies of the prison cell and the brutal Special Branch interrogators she encountered. “In prison, you only see the moves of the enemy,” she later recalled. “Prison is the hardest place to fight a battle.” 117 Days provided a firsthand sense of political incarceration with its gendered and racial dimensions, its psychological challenges through solitary confinement, and its potential for new forms of solidarity. Above all, her account raised a set of fundamental questions. What counted as a “crime” in apartheid South Africa? Who are the victims? Who are the perpetrators? Who is the law for? Where is justice in a situation where the law and morality are diametrically opposed to one another? Exile Released in December 1963, First left South Africa in March 1964, never to return. She was greeted as a celebrity when she arrived in London with her daughters Robyn and Gillian. Yet, as with many others, exile proved to be a complex experience — personally liberating, but at the price of losing touch with one’s homeland. Exile could be long and rife with uncertainty. London was disorienting for First, not just culturally but also because of the new sense of freedom and agency she had. Political work competed with domestic responsibilities. The so-called external mission of the ANC involved diplomatic trips and speeches at numerous venues. Still, though her ongoing activism provided a point of orientation, it was her intellectual work that blossomed. In exile, First’s experience as a journalist translated into longer works of scholarship and political theory after the publication of 117 Days . Above all, First’s writing grappled with questions that animated the policy discussions and debates among ANC and SACP members. Her first book, South West Africa , published in 1963 before she left for exile, presented a critical appraisal of South Africa’s control over what is today Namibia. In effect, the book presented a more expansive engagement with the concept of “colonialism of a special type” by examining South Africa’s colonial rule of the former German territory, which had been granted under the League of Nations mandate system after World War I. First’s later books similarly confronted and tested party ideas through different contexts, as well as through the lens of her personal experience. Her 1980 biography of Olive Schreiner (coauthored with Ann Scott) addressed the life and politics of one of South Africa’s most important socialist intellectuals, a study that undoubtedly held meaning for First. The Mozambican Miner: Proletarian and Peasant , published posthumously in 1983, contributed to discussions of racial capitalism in the wider region of southern Africa. However, it is First’s 1970 book , The Barrel of a Gun: Political Power in Africa and the Coup d’État , which stands out as her major contribution to the literature of revolution and postcolonial political theory. On the surface, it is an account of coups in postindependence Africa, with case studies drawn from Sudan, Nigeria, and Ghana. The book is not an armchair retelling of these episodes. First traveled extensively to gain firsthand knowledge on the ground. As she wrote, she wanted The Barrel of a Gun to be attuned to “the sense of pulsating life in the streets” and to reflect “something of the way people see, and say things about, their condition.” The Barrel of a Gun also reveals a deeper subtext with its focus on African militaries and their political power. First’s keen interest in the topic was shaped by her involvement in the formation of MK and the anti-apartheid movement’s turn to armed struggle. Indeed, her personal papers reveal an early optimistic view of armies as a revolutionary vanguard that gradually shifted as her research progressed. Her conclusions in The Barrel of Gun are very different, underscoring how postcolonial militaries are much more ambiguous in their character. At times, coups could speed up the process of political change to positive ends by ending autocratic regimes. But they could also do the exact opposite by establishing authoritarian rule. First’s most important contribution is to underline the legacy of colonialism in fostering the conditions for postcolonial political instability. In his classic work, How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972), Walter Rodney forcefully argued how centuries of European colonialism set back the continent from an economic standpoint. In The Barrel of a Gun , First likewise argues that European colonialism politically underdeveloped Africa, by leaving weak institutions that were vulnerable to military takeover. For this reason, among many, The Barrel of a Gun still stands as a foundational diagnosis of postcolonial Africa in the years immediately following decolonization. Legacies If The Barrel of a Gun marked a certain culmination of First’s thinking, it was certainly not the final answer to her questions about the vicissitudes of political power and the possibilities of revolution in Africa. Her book Libya: The Elusive Revolution , published a few years later in 1974, is a provisional sequel to The Barrel of a Gun , examining the opportunities and limits of the coup that brought Muammar Gaddafi to power in 1969. However, it was the liberation of Mozambique from Portuguese colonial rule in 1975 that opened a new horizon for First. Neighboring South Africa and led by the Marxist-Leninist Front for the Liberation of Mozambique (FRELIMO), independent Mozambique presented her with an opportunity to witness a revolution in southern Africa as it was unfolding. It provided her with a chance to live out her revolutionary ideals. This period of optimism for First, lived in the belief that a Marxist-Leninist revolution would soon cross the border into her native South Africa, proved all too short. The police unit whose members interrogated her in 1963 was the same unit that organized her assassination almost two decades later. Despite her premature passing at the age of fifty-seven, First’s writing and political example live on. Though committed to the South African cause and communism as a political worldview, her work avoided the parochialism of many nationalist thinkers, as well as the constraints of Marxist orthodoxy. Her vision remained expansive by considering case studies beyond South Africa, yet it aligned with questions that preoccupied her comrades and friends in the SACP and the ANC. Like the work of Frantz Fanon, who was a crucial influence for her, First’s perspectives and ideas endure because they were born in the unstable crucible of active struggle, not the sequestered institutional spaces of academia or the conformist atmospheres of party offices. Though the revolution First imagined for South Africa has not occurred, with the two-stage program of the long-ago Native Republic thesis only partly fulfilled, the questions she raised for her country and her continent continue: What is the nature of political power? What is the role of the state in the lives of ordinary people? What is the role of violence in liberation or oppression? How can the lives of workers, both women and men, receive justice? And, finally, what are the conditions for revolution, and what does revolution mean in practice? These questions and the force of politics behind them still deserve answers.

articles.title: Private Equity’s Pension Heist
articles.author: Clark Randall
articles.content: From 2024 to 2025, the two hundred largest pension funds in the United States increased their investment in private credit by 57 percent . It’s now gone up around 650 percent over the past five years. Private credit is the other side of the coin to private equity (PE) — among other things, it provides the loans for PE firms’ leveraged buyouts. The biggest PE firms have massive private credit arms that have, in recent years, overrun their private equity cores. They act as the unregulated winners of the postrecession economy, avoiding scrutiny and taking risks that commercial banks were foreclosed from under the Dodd–Frank Act. Our worker-funded public pensions have historically been the primary capital provider to private credit funds, amounting to around 30 percent of the total market. Many of these same private credit funds have found themselves in a world of trouble over the past twelve months, just as public pensions have loaded them up with increasing capital. The chief investment officer at New York City retirement systems recently told the Financial Times , “We have completely committed to private credit, we are willing to trade illiquidity and complexity for a higher return.” As is the case in all investing, higher ceilings come with lower floors. Credit defaults, according to Fitch ratings, are hitting record highs and nonaccrual status loans, i.e., ones where borrowers are in serious trouble, spiked 40 percent since this March. In response to these issues on the borrower end, private credit funds have extended their lockup period, put hard-line caps on redemptions to prevent runs on capital, and opened up investment to 401(k) holders and individuals to increase capital inflows. It’s unclear whether we have a total crisis on our hands, in part due to shady reporting standards at pension funds, but it is clear that we have a real problem in private credit regardless. The issue is downstream of the problem in private equity where holding periods are up, and by extension, the net asset value (NAV) of funds held over seven years (sometimes referred to as “zombie funds”) has doubled since 2021 . They can’t sell the asset, so they build continuation vehicles to recapitalize and hide the struggle that’s going on. But the real risk of this slowdown weighs on retirees, current and future. When it comes to pension funds, the fees charged by private credit and alternative investment writ large (hedge funds, real estate, and private equity) are unknown to the public. They are also not Freedom of Information Act–eligible, due to bogus trade-secret protections claimed by local governments. That means workers are barred from understanding what their own contributions are going toward. Even if we don’t have smoking guns, instead we have mounting circumstantial evidence that our public pensions are robbed of investment returns by the growth of alternative asset investing and the dark hole of management and performance fee structures. In explaining this problem, the new film Pension Fight Club offers a good, but at times awkwardly laid-out, documentary for those interested in deciphering the relationship between workers’ capital and the excesses of finance capital. Impasse The story of the documentary is twofold: the first being the misrepresentation of investment fees by public pension funds due to either ignorance or quid pro quo exchanges between investment consultants and political officials. We have the example of the Minnesota public pension fund that, following Ted Siedle’s investigation, shifted their investment fee total from $11 million to $188 million across a three-year period. What pension funds often do is report on the fee for assets under management but not the performance fee or the carried interest. That is, after surpassing a set hurdle rate, alternative investment managers take somewhere in the range of 20 percent of profits thereafter. Pension funds don’t count that as investment fees despite the fact that it eats into their rate of return. What’s more: if a pension fund commits $100 million to an alternative investment manager, they pay them for total assets under management, not assets deployed — so, $30 million might sit idly while the pension fund paid a premium for the full amount to be actively managed. The second is the bigger picture: that is, the political economy of public pensions. From political donations to stack the board to investment decisions, public pensions operate in a world of information asymmetry. Those on the inside understand its influence, and everyone else is not let in on the potential costs of pension investment underperformance, the risk of complex exposure, and the behind-the-scenes nature of decision-making. From 2001–2023, fully 99 percent of pension plans failed to meet their assumed rates of return over that period in the aggregate. That means that actuarial calculations of what these funds owe are misunderstood at best and severely underestimated at worst. Despite this overreporting of assets on hand, cities are still spending increasing portions of their budgets paying down pension debt. Sarah Anzia, leading scholar on public pensions, found that over a quarter of US cities and counties more than doubled their nominal pension expenditures between 2005–2016 alone. The context, however, is an era of underfunding, punting, or kicking the can down the road on pension contributions and “ looting the funds ” amid the aftermath of the Great Recession. Still, Anzia’s findings back the concern of the film, demonstrating that public pension troubles are not quite ubiquitous, but they’re intractable once felt. Pension Fight Club traces the impasse facing public pensions. It portrays a dilemma, over whether these funds reveal their exposure to alternative investments and the fees they pay for them or else continue to kick the can down the road as economic conditions tighten. The film depicts the political incentives, bribes, faux policy fixes, and shrouded accounting that make public pensions both the willing and unwitting prey to the new Wall Street — as explored in Brett Christophers’s 2023 book , Our Lives in Their Portfolios . Still, it’s also true that this documentary stumbles in narrativizing a complex story. It jumps from one fund to another, and their struggles with opaque investment policies but leaves the viewer too attached to a singular node, Ted Siedle, as he investigates fund policies — when a larger story could have been told about unions’ (collective) struggles to direct capital investment. It’s a story that is itself complicated enough, showing that finance fixed almost as many issues as it caused unions historically, and can be followed through the work scholars like Michael McCarthy and Brian Judge . In any case, the documentary brings important attention to public pensions and what the years ahead may have in store considering how they invested after the recession. Uphill Struggle Strapped with steep investment losses, surging unfunded liabilities, a shrinking public workforce, and cash-strapped local governments following the 2008 crash, public pension funds wanted out of a hole, fast. Distressed assets flooded the market and private equity, real estate investment trusts, and private credit were there to sweep it up in multifarious, intersecting mechanisms, front the costs, and offload the risk to creditors or the governing bodies they were purchasing from. In this regard, it’s useful to take another look at Christophers’s chapter on the infamous sale of Chicago’s parking meters and underground lots to Morgan Stanley, which resulted in an immediate cash drain on the city. Still, what Christophers’s account misses is that the Illinois Municipal Retirement Fund (IMRF) — the largest in the state — in the prior year’s (2007’s) disclosures , reported over $100 million invested in a Morgan Stanley real estate fund and $17 million in their public stock. The dots don’t always connect in a straight line, but the same story is now decades old: public pensions are funding their own gravediggers . These investments routinely grow the wealth of right-wing, anti-union oligarchs and their corporate monopolies. The fight in Pension Fight Club is as much against the alt-investment managers’ operations as it is the uphill battle to convince the public, especially those without pensions, that banal local pension policies matter. Pension funds are no longer bundled up in fixed-income municipal bonds and Treasuries. Nor are they simply overexposed to equities, which they are and were in the lead-up to 2008. Public pensions acted as the underwriters to an absurd new class of private equity multimillionaires and billionaires — the new power brokers on Wall Street and Silicon Valley. When the Los Angeles Lakers sold to a venture capital consortium recently for a jaw-dropping $12.5 billion, it was a final signal for the sports world that private equity is here to stay. The team’s historic rival, the Boston Celtics, also sold to private equity players for $6 billion a year prior. But where did Joshua Kushner’s (brother of Jared’s) Thrive Capital get its seed funding to make such a purchase? Of the first billion it raised, $300 million came from a CalPERS investment , that is, from California’s state pension fund. To put the matter truthfully but a little too plainly, the workers now own a stake in the Lakers, even though none of them can afford to attend a game at the new Crypto.com Arena. The Pension Fight Club documentary offers valuable evidence that there’s a long way to go in the push-and-pull between reform and deregulation in the field of workers’ capital. My sense is that if the movement to unearth pension funds’ investments remains limited to union activism and siloed lawyers alone, it may not be enough. Any taxpaying resident has good reason to care about how pensions are invested. The first reason is that shoring up these policies will lighten the tax load on local governments which are losing money; the second is the need to quell the idea that pensions are “unaffordable” due to what retirees are being paid. Pensions are a functional structure in need of serious repair, and the crisis can hardly be blamed on meager cost-of-living adjustments or sweeteners offered to working-class retirees. While the media latches onto stories of superintendents and administrators earning six-figure pensions to characterize the problem, the majority of retirees with pensions are bringing in under $40,000. This is a crisis of short-term governance, financial capture, and the unaccountability of this industry.

articles.title: Francis Fukuyama: The American Right Has Gone Off the Deep End
articles.author: Francis Fukuyama
articles.content: In 1989, Francis Fukuyama wrote a sweeping philosophical polemic in which he argued that liberal democratic capitalism was the only viable economic and political system. Countries would either converge on its model or drift into dysfunction. What prevented states and individuals from accepting this fate was a fear of being the Last Man, a Nietzschean term for the individual living without ideas worth dying for. A world in which liberal democracy was triumphant was, Fukuyama argued in “The End of History?,” one without the tragedy and pathos of the era of great ideologies — safe but boring.f When he expanded this essay three years later into The End of History and the Last Man , Fukuyama gave voice to a worry that this condition of placid stability may not be able to satisfy the drives of all individuals. Here he echoed G. W. F. Hegel, the philosopher from whom he took the idea of a universal history, who wrote that “within the state, heroes are no longer possible: they occur only in the absence of civilization.” In his upcoming memoir, In the Realm of the Last Man , Fukuyama makes clear that he views figures like Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump as unwilling to pay the cost of progress. They instead hearken back to a time of heroic conflict, refusing to accept the constraints of liberal democratic capitalism. Jacobin spoke to Fukuyama about his own intellectual development from a former Republican policy adviser to the Ronald Reagan administration and member of the RAND Corporation to a Democrat who now describes himself as, with some qualifications, a social democrat. In this interview, Fukuyama also discusses the transformations of the American right, what the Democratic left could learn from Trump, and from Zohran Mamdani’s successes in New York. John-Baptiste Oduor You were about sixteen in 1968 and became a conservative a few years later at Cornell. How did you think about yourself in relationship to the progressive and leftist politics of that period? Did you think you were reacting against them? Francis Fukuyama It was really my teachers at Cornell, particularly Allan Bloom — they were all students of Leo Strauss — who influenced me during that period. Strauss made a complex set of arguments, but basically he argued that the Western philosophical tradition had gotten itself into a dead end with the rise of the relativism that was the core of the teaching of people like Friedrich Nietzsche and Martin Heidegger. That was a problem because people still had moral commitments, which were necessary for society. Strauss argued that it was still possible to use human reason to come to an understanding of basic issues of good and bad that progressive thought had, in a certain way, rejected. I spent a lot of time as an undergraduate going back to Plato and Aristotle because that’s the core of the Western project to use reason to answer big questions about the nature of justice, the nature of human happiness, and so forth. That was really what I was doing when I was an undergraduate. And it wasn’t in reaction to progressivism in particular. I mean, it was a very turbulent time in American politics because the Vietnam War was raging. There was a lot of student activism. And I participated in some of that. Probably my sophomore or junior year, I went to an anti–Vietnam War protest in Washington, DC. John-Baptiste Oduor What in your view was the political content of Straussian conservatism then? Figures like Patrick Deneen and Michael Anton who are close to the current administration take it to imply an ethnonationalist view of Western cultural traditions. Francis Fukuyama I think they have taken a really ridiculous position. I have debated Deneen in the past few years a couple of times. Many people who consider themselves in some way students of Leo Strauss split into different factions. One of the big divisions is between so-called West Coast traditions associated with the Claremont Institute and East Coast students who were more likely to be students of Allan Bloom or possibly Harvey Mansfield. The West Coast traditions, in my view, have just gone off the deep end. A lot of [thinkers associated with them], like Michael Anton, have become die-hard Trump supporters. They’ve forgotten a lot of the basic teachings of people who were students of Strauss like Harry Jaffa, who was really the founder of that whole West Coast school. Patrick Deneen, I think, has discovered a certain celebrity by arguing that we ought to go back before the Enlightenment, to a period when Western countries were united by a single conservative Catholic doctrine. It’s totally absurd that anyone could think this was remotely possible in the year 2026. I don’t associate myself with any of those particular schools. I remain what I regard as a classical liberal, meaning that I believe that liberal democracy is the only practical way to govern a modern society. John-Baptiste Oduor American conservatism has taken an anti-humanist turn over the past ten to fifteen years, particularly under the influence of the tech right. How do you think this happened? Francis Fukuyama I think it’s a complicated story. The person who has written the most intelligently about this is Laura Field. She published a book last year called Furious Minds , where she traces the origins of a lot of this. I believe her account that a lot of this is people who are American nationalists, in some sense, who have dressed up their politics in a theoretical language to defend something that’s just basically American chauvinism. That is part of it. The other part is the opportunism of people who saw Trump rising. They saw that this was a powerful real-world political force that they wanted to attach themselves to. And so, for the last ten years they’ve been tying themselves in knots trying to come up with a highbrow philosophical justification for Trumpism. It just doesn’t work, because I don’t think Trumpism is a coherent doctrine. It’s just the psychopathology of this one individual. All of these theoretical attempts to put him into some a structured framework are bound to fail. People like Peter Thiel and J. D. Vance are good examples. Thiel has started to use this theological language about the Antichrist to explain what Trumpism is about. I think that’s all silly. It’s not serious political theory. John-Baptiste Oduor Speaking of J. D. Vance, figures like him and Tucker Carlson have at points tried to present Trumpism as part of a redistributive pro-worker conservatism. In practice, the politics of the Republican Party has been the same as it has always been: tax cuts and war. Do you have an explanation of why this pro-worker conservatism has so little foothold in reality? Francis Fukuyama In many ways, it was displaced workers in depressed, postindustrial parts of the country that formed part of the original Trump coalition. And I think it’s true that the Democrats and a lot of liberals didn’t do a whole lot for them. Democrats were the ones who were pushing the North American Free Trade Agreement and these different trade liberalization deals that led to the elimination of their jobs. When China was let into the World Trade Organization, it cost a couple million manufacturing jobs. The Democrats did little to combat this. Trump’s voter base was motivated partly by resentment against this. Culturally, also, the Democratic Party moved into a very different space than these voters. Previously, it had been made up of a coalition in which working-class people were a major component. This was true from the 1930s on. But gradually, as you got closer to the twenty-first century, elites within the Democratic Party became college-educated professionals. Culturally, I think they speak a different language from most working-class Americans. I think a lot of those working-class people began to perceive that, culturally, they didn’t have anything to do with the leadership of the Democratic Party. And this came to a head particularly on issues like immigration, where the elites in the party were just taking a very different attitude from a lot of working-class people who weren’t in favor of open borders. John-Baptiste Oduor How did this coalition that mobilized around issues like open borders and police abolition that — bracketing their soundness — were quite unpopular among working-class Americans become so prominent within the Democratic Party? This variant of progressivism has always existed but has never become as dominant as it became in the 2010s. Francis Fukuyama I don’t have a good explanation for this other than a general failure of leadership. Nancy Pelosi, when she was speaker, used to talk about “the groups” in the Democratic Party, meaning that there were just several dozen different small factions within the party representing environmentalists, African Americans, immigrants, disabled people, and others. No Democratic politician could survive going against any one of these groups. They would have to go around basically affirming their agenda. I think that this speaks to a lack of leadership, because what was needed was a leader on the Left to say: we have to prioritize, and we’re not going to satisfy the interests of all these different little factions within the Democratic Party. But you never really had that leadership emerge. I think maybe it’s beginning to happen. One of the big divisions in the party was between those who were focused, like Bernie Sanders, on economic-equality issues, and others that were more interested in identity politics. Those two wings have been contesting ever since. And it may now be the case that more of the progressive left is shifting more toward an economic focus, which, by the way, I think would be a good thing. John-Baptiste Oduor In a recent essay, you discussed Trump’s attempts to consolidate executive power, motivated by a theory of a unified executive. One of the potential consequences of the success of this project would, you write, be the emergence of a “spoils” system. What would this look like? Francis Fukuyama I’m not sure Trump himself has a coherent understanding of this, but certainly people like Russell Vought, who’s now the head of the Office of Management and Budget, has ideas. It’s all based on an irrational hatred of government. Vought believes the permanent bureaucracy is full of left-wing ideologues who really don’t respond to a democratic choice. This is complete nonsense. If you look at the history of the American bureaucracy in the nineteenth century, you had the spoils system, or the patronage system, where virtually every federal employee was there because of a political favor from a politician. This was changed only beginning in 1883, with the passage of the Pendleton Act, which created a civil service commission. This made it so that you needed to take a civil service exam or have some credentials in order to work for the US government. This didn’t suit the interests of the politicians at the time. It took the assassination of President James Garfield in 1881 by an office seeker to shame Congress into passing the Pendleton Act. But slowly, we developed a professional civil service that operated according to the principle that a civil servant is not a partisan. They exist to implement the wishes of democratically elected leaders, and they do so no matter which party is in power. As the federal government expanded in the 1930s and became much more complex, the expertise of these bureaucrats became much more important. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Federal Aviation Administration, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration — you have all these new agencies that really can’t be run by political partisans. The staff of the Federal Reserve is full of PhD economists and people with long experience in financial markets. This expansion of expertise is inevitable in a modern economy. You cannot run a government without this expertise, but there’s been this huge populist revolt against the very idea of expertise. There’s very little appreciation on the Right for the fact that you actually do need medical professionals to run a public health service, this sort of thing. The rise of the internet has promoted all of these really wild conspiracy theories. The number of Americans that think that the COVID-19 vaccine was causing more death than COVID itself . . . it’s shocking. But I should say, before I go further, that there was something to the unhappiness with the existing bureaucracy, because it did actually become very difficult to control a lot of bureaucrats. Public sector unions that wanted to protect jobs were really powerful. Compared to the private sector, if you wanted to discipline an employee in a federal agency, it was much harder to do that than in a private company. This created an excessive rigidity, but that does not justify this wholesale attack on expertise and on the idea of a neutral public service, which is really core to the way any modern government has to operate. John-Baptiste Oduor The critique of state bureaucracy is a long-running one. A version of it can be found in the Mancur Olson’s book The Rise and Decline of Nations . He was concerned with rent-seeking coalitions, but a version of this critique has recently resurfaced in the so-called abundance movement. Do you think some of the strength of the MAGA project has come from the Left’s unwillingness to take seriously concerns about the calcified nature of bureaucracies under democracies? Francis Fukuyama I think that’s right. The problem is not that the bureaucrats themselves are calcified. They’re simply responding to the incentives created by the system and to the rules that have been established as a result of pressure or actual state capture by a lot of very powerful interest groups. That’s what’s made it very difficult to do things like build sufficient affordable housing or to build infrastructure in a timely, inexpensive way. The history here is complicated, but there’s a very insightful book by Mark Dunkelman called Why Nothing Works that places a certain amount of the blame for this on the Left — the progressive left, because in the Progressive era and through to the 1950s, many progressives felt that government was the main engine for social progress. The Tennessee Valley Authority, the Hoover Dam, and the Works Progress Administration: these are all federal-government-led efforts to get the economy going again. But beginning in the 1960s, with the rise of the public interest movement led by people like Ralph Nader, a lot of progressives began to argue that actually the government was the problem, that the government had been captured by corporations and was no longer representing the people but was actually defending these entrenched corporate interests. And honestly, that was true in a lot of sectors, but I think that this skepticism toward the state led to a convergence of the Left and the Right. The Right always hated government, and the Left began to be very suspicious of big government as well. Fundamentally, what the abundance movement wants to do is to try to change that cultural mindset, to say, no, actually, government can be a force for change. If you’re going to decarbonize the American economy, it can’t be driven by grassroots movements. It really does require much stronger action to build transmission lines and to incentivize alternative energy. John-Baptiste Oduor But doesn’t capital also need to be disciplined? The discussion around abundance has been couched in terms of removing bureaucratic hurdles and getting rid of rent-seeking mediators. But that on its own is not enough. Francis Fukuyama I think you need a middle position where you can admit that many things, particularly the way that bureaucrats are forced to operate, are overregulated and yet say that the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and the Republican solution is not a solution. You need rules. There are good reasons why you’ve got worker-safety and environmental protections and all sort of limits on what the government can do and how it needs to operate. But you can also make them more flexible and easier to implement. I’ll just give you a concrete example. If a federal agency wants to buy an office computer or a desk, it has to comply with something called the federal acquisitions regulations, which are literally hundreds of pages of detailed rules about how you buy stuff in the federal government. No private corporation has to deal with that volume of rules, which were originally put in place to prevent corruption. But you don’t need hundreds and hundreds of pages of regulations in order to get to that objective. Something similar is true, I think, with environmental law. The National Environmental Policy Act was very important. It set the model for environmental protection by mandating the need for environmental reviews. And that was necessary. But over time, the length of these reviews has grown so that today they are thousands of pages long and take five or even ten years to write. That adds dramatically to the cost of building infrastructure. John-Baptiste Oduor During Trump’s first term, the tariffs he imposed on China were treated as extreme policies at the time, but they have now become part of the center ground of American politics, for better or worse. In his second term, Trump has now expanded the power of the executive. Do you envision this new view of executive power as becoming a new norm for both parties? Could the progressive wing of the Democratic Party use these powers to enact policies that its base wants? Francis Fukuyama This is something that progressives need to think about very carefully, because checks and balances work in both directions. They are a protection against a would-be authoritarian like Trump, but they also limit what a good progressive administration would like to achieve. You actually saw this under both Barack Obama and Joe Biden, where a lot of the things they wanted to do, like Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, had to be done by executive order. The cancellation of student debt under Biden was done by an executive order because they could not get this stuff through Congress. There is a temptation to simply do things unilaterally using the executive. If there’s a progressive president elected in 2028, there will be a strong temptation to continue to exercise the executive powers that Trump has been using. That’s a danger. It’s easy to get frustrated with checks and balances and then say, we’re just going to cut through all this bullshit and get stuff done. I think that mindset is helpful in certain instances, because there is a lot of unnecessary bureaucratic constraint on governments, but fundamentally you need a rule of law. John-Baptiste Oduor In The End of History and the Last Man , you offered a psychological explanation of the drive to break with liberal capitalism. The term you used was a Greek one, thumos , which you interpreted to be a drive for recognition. It lay, you argued there and also in your new book, in a refusal to accept our posthistorical condition — a refusal to be the Last Man. Is it fair to say that in your view, both the Left and the Right, insofar as they reject the essential role of an apolitical bureaucracy, checks on executive power, and the rule of law are regressing to a preliberal form of politics that is inherently unsustainable? Francis Fukuyama I don’t want to psychologize people on the Left at the present moment, because first of all, I think that there’s a very diverse set of interests represented there. And I’m not sure that resorting to psychology as opposed to discussing policy and this sort of thing is really helpful. But it’s certainly true about the Right. Right now, it is very hard to discern any consistent set of ideas or ideology that defines what Trump is trying to do. You have to resort to individual psychology. You know that this is a guy that has grown up with all these resentments and prejudices. He felt that he was grievously persecuted after he left office, and he wants to get revenge. He also doesn’t know very much about foreign policy. After he captured Nicolás Maduro, he suddenly realized he had this great power to act militarily on the world stage. Now he’s gotten us into this unnecessary war with Iran a result. You can’t explain that through theories like isolationism or realism or any of the terms that are used by international relations experts to characterize these underlying trends. You need to look to the weird psychology of this one individual. That is completely a matter of thumos. Thumos is the feeling of being disrespected and desperately trying to gain that respect, oftentimes by claiming power and dominance. I think that’s really what’s going on. There are two individuals who suffered this when Obama was president. One was Trump, at this White House Correspondents’ Dinner, where Obama made fun of him and he had to slink off with his tail between his legs. The other was Vladimir Putin. Obama at one point characterized Russia as a regional power, not a global great power. Now, this is an exaggeration, but I think that both of these individuals after those episodes bore this incredible resentment that they were not being taken seriously by the world’s leading democracy. A lot of their subsequent behavior has to be explained in terms of their wanting to prove their detractors wrong. John-Baptiste Oduor Aren’t there longer-term trends at work driving the behavior of Russia and the United States? Under the Obama administration, there was talk of a “pivot to Asia,” which is in part a justification for Trump’s hawkishness. And the Republican Party has long been frustrated with what it saw as the incoherence of Obama’s Iran deal. Many rightly saw the partial rapprochement as incompatible with maintaining healthy relations with Israel. Francis Fukuyama At a certain level, all of these policies could be justified in terms of a hyperrealist view of the world as full of dangerous enemies. But I think that the particular way that Trump has engaged in these arenas speaks to something different that isn’t coming out of the realm of ideas. For example, one of the remarkable things about the Iran war is that he discarded all of the process that usually guides American foreign policy. Now, you may say that in the past that process produced bad results like the Iraq War. And that’s true. But at least there was some effort to systematically think about second- and third-order consequences. Questions like, how did this affect the economy? How did this affect our allies? And so forth. Even if that did not prevent the Iraq War from happening, it certainly prepared the United States in certain ways for what was to come. There are plenty of people in the US national security establishment who would have told Trump that if you attack Iran in that direct manner, it’s going to try to close the Strait of Hormuz because that’s their big trump card. Plenty of people could have told the Trump administration that. Trump simply was listening to Steve Witkoff, his son-in-law Jared Kushner, and his very small group of people that agreed with him. John-Baptiste Oduor One of our frequent contributors, Paul Heideman , recently wrote a book, Rogue Elephant , in which he argued that the extreme turn of the Republican Party is a consequence of their success: Having defeated organized labor, they no longer had a need to organize businesses into a coherent coalition. This disorganization of the Right allowed minoritarian interests to take hold of the Republican Party. Do you find this plausible? Francis Fukuyama Yes. It’s plausible in the sense that in most liberal democracies in the 1950s and ’60s up through the ’70s, there was a social contract that said organized labor does have to be incorporated into public decision-making. In Germany, still to this day, wages are set by nationally coordinated bargaining between the big German companies and the labor unions. That’s also true in Scandinavia. It’s true in a lot of European countries. And we in the Unted States had an informal understanding — as a result of all the labor strife in the 1930s — by the 1950s that major firms, like big car companies, had to work with the United Auto Workers and that sort of thing. Ronald Reagan really undermined the position of organized labor. I would say to that extent, what you’ve said is probably an accurate reading of what has happened. John-Baptiste Oduor You’ve moved to the left in the past few two decades. But the Republican Party has also moved very far in the opposite direction. Do you still think about yourself as a conservative? Francis Fukuyama I don’t think of myself as a conservative, really. I think of myself as a classic social democrat. You have to have a market economy. It needs to be carefully regulated, and you need a certain amount of redistribution because otherwise you’re not going to have a stable political system. I think that was the winning formula for much of the post–World War II period. Getting away from that is one of the reasons that things have become so unstable in our politics. On certain cultural issues, I find myself more on the conservative side. I wrote a whole book about identity politics, which I believe is very problematic. But certainly, on the economic issues, I wouldn’t say that I’m a conservative. John-Baptiste Oduor Finally, what do you make of Zohran Mamdani and the prospect of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez potentially running for president? Francis Fukuyama I think Mamdani has been very careful and politically pretty smart. He’s embraced part of the abundance movement because he realizes that you do need to deliver these sorts of concrete results.
