If politicians like him or AOC are able to break free of some of the existing constraints that they currently face, what their agenda would be remains an open question. There I don’t know what the answer is. You’ll have to tell me. There are certainly people on the left wing of the Democratic Party who, I think, are just out to lunch and dangerous, like Hasan Piker. But if you tell me that he’s not going to have any real policy influence, then ok.

articles.title: In Serbia, Few Frankly Reckon With Ratko Mladić’s Crimes
articles.author: Lela Vujanić
articles.content: When residents of a block in Belgrade’s city center woke up to the news last week, they were confronted with a mural celebrating a war criminal, painted overnight. Furious, they plotted a “night action” to destroy this latest tribute to Ratko Mladić with improvised defacement tactics. While the war criminal’s face is ever present across the Serbian capital, this was the first time a mural several meters long and about one meter high had appeared on the building surrounding their park. The news of Mladić’s death, while in detention at The Hague, came in the middle of a campaign for parliamentary elections that have not yet been called but according to President Aleksandar Vučić are expected any day now. What a popular slogan calls the “students who are winning” (after a series of recent mass protests) are campaigning for the vote, as are the current head of state Vučić and his SNS (the Serbian Progressive Party, in name only). The justice minister hastily announced that “the protocols are known” and that Mladić, being a general, would be buried accordingly, with military and state honors. Still, Vučić, the all-powerful president, backed away while pointing to “family wishes” and suggesting there might be no state-sponsored funeral. A few opposition leaders issued statements firmly distancing themselves from Mladić’s legacy and emphasizing the need not to forget or relativize the truth about his victims and the genocide. The European Commission, which is not exactly a moral or political authority here, said there is no room for an EU candidate country to celebrate a convicted war criminal. In Republika Srpska — the Bosnian Serb entity within neighboring Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Mladić commanded atrocities — numerous vigils were held, often featuring well-known football hooligan iconography. In a professionally produced video, students from Republika Srpska in Belgrade held up a huge poster over the Branko Bridge depicting Mladić, bearing the words “From your struggle, our freedom lives.” Survivors and victims’ associations from the genocide site at Srebrenica and across Bosnia were once again shocked at such reactions. While approving of Mladić’s sentence and imprisonment, they pointed out that his death changes nothing. It does not bring the dead back or erase the mass graves. Myth-Building Amid the Breakup of Yugoslavia Ratko Mladić was born in eastern Bosnia in 1942. He joined the Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) in 1965, when it was still a widely respected institution of socialist Yugoslavia. He climbed steadily through its ranks, eventually becoming a general. Yet his real ascent began with the breakup of Yugoslavia at the turn of the 1990s. He started building his reputation in Knin, where he was sent to fight the forces of newly independent Croatia. When the JNA decided to officially withdraw from Bosnia and the Army of Republika Srpska was formed in 1992, he was appointed commander of its Main Staff, inheriting much of the JNA local infrastructure, including personnel, weaponry, and other resources. Media-savvy and always ready for the camera, Mladić switched his ideological allegiances — from defender of socialist Yugoslavia to an ethnically attuned defender of Serbs and their land. His wartime legacy in Bosnia included the siege of Sarajevo, the genocide in Srebrenica, and war crimes and crimes against humanity across different parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. After the Dayton Peace Agreement in 1995 marked the end of the war in Bosnia, he was indicted by the United Nations’ International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY). Avoiding trial, he came to Belgrade and lived fairly openly under Slobodan Milošević’s protection until his patron fell in October 2000. He spent the following years in hiding — first aided by a network of former military officers and later by relatives, vanishing from public view entirely by 2008. He was finally captured in 2011 in a village in northern Serbia and extradited to The Hague. He died this August 27 in a prison hospital. No matter what his physical location or his administrative or carceral status, Mladić was present in Serbia all along, as a ready-made poster, mural, slogan, T-shirt icon, overarching symbol, or historical and narrative arc, to be used and reused in endless political and (social) media campaigns. He was ready to serve, dead or alive. He remains a crucial part of government-linked street and hooligan groups’ mass-scale visual campaigns , regularly performed across Belgrade. Tanja Marković, an activist involved in peace and antifascist initiatives since the 1990s, told me: “The state maintains no distance whatsoever. We remember how it guarded the Ratko Mladić mural in Njegoševa, in an organized fashion, and how long it took for that mural to be removed.” Some of the most enduring slogans are those related to genocide: “The only genocide in the Balkans was against the Serbs,” read a huge piece of graffiti, in English, on a building in the city’s main avenue, just across from the Belgrade Cultural Center. Then there are those depicting Mladić, usually featured in close-up, wearing an army hat or, in the case of graffiti, there is simply his name accompanied by an “appropriate” slogan. These murals and slogans often provoke rage among other citizens and peace and youth activists, who throw eggs or try covering them with white paint, only for the murals to resurface again. In nationalist myth, Mladić serves as a defender, preventing a new genocide against the Serbs, within a historical arc that connects the slaughter of Serbs in World War II with the real and threatened ethnic cleansing of Serbs during the Yugoslav Wars. He not only defended Serbs from domestic enemies, such as Croats and Muslims, but from imperialist forces too. Anti-NATO is always a great story hook, especially in Serbia, which was later depleted by sanctions and subjected to the highly controversial NATO bombing campaign ( precedent for which were air strikes against Mladić’s forces in 1995). With a quasi-socialist pivot at first, then transitioning to ethnonationalism with an anti-imperialist flavor, the myth resolves complex histories and some real grievances into a murderous, single-hero story that plays well within a wider narrative framework centered on ancient ethnic wounds and hatred. This framework explains not only the war but also how and why socialist Yugoslavia broke up. Contrary to all the data on mass impoverishment , we did not lose a class war but simply so terribly and murderously hated each other. Genocide Denial to Stay in Power There are only two questions that every contender for political power in Serbia has to answer: Was there a genocide in Srebrenica, and is Kosovo Serbia? Whoever the challenger and whatever they really think, you can always see them being grilled in those TV debate chairs, playing an impossible game rigged to ensure any myth-busters will lose the part that matters: i.e., the elections. For an outsider, both questions could appear not only morally corrupt but intellectually delusional. Kosovo, with or without asterisks (Kosovo*, as it is sometimes styled in the official international documents), does exist. And the genocide in Srebrenica did happen; we could hardly miss the bones of the thousands of victims, brushed clean by forensic experts as they were recovered and identified from mass graves, including the secondary ones, where bodies had been moved and scattered in an attempt to cover up the crime. There were times in Serbia’s recent history when it seemed that society was ready to confront its past and begin rebuilding relations with its neighbors. When rereading the articles and rewatching TV, it is obvious that even Radio Television of Serbia, the public broadcaster, though always under the strong grip of whichever party was in power, did in multiple programs offer its viewers insight into the scale of the atrocities and the burden that this legacy places on those living. In 2010, the Serbian parliament adopted a declaration condemning the crime in Srebrenica, offering an apology and condolences to the families of the victims for the failure to prevent the tragedy. Vučić himself went to Srebrenica for the twentieth-anniversary commemoration in 2015, marking a shift toward reconciliation compared to his earlier political stance. Why then, does the myth persist? Who benefits from it? Who is keeping it alive? Who can break it down and introduce a new myth? In 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution commemorating the Srebrenica genocide, explicitly condemning genocide denial and the glorification of those convicted for war crimes. On the day of the vote, Vučić was at the UN, wrapped in a Serbian flag, his posture as if in prayer for Serbia not to be charged with genocide. During the evening, a skyscraper that is part of a highly dubious urbanistic mega project, Belgrade Waterfront, which also serves as a visual campaign booth, fluorescently flashed the words “We are not genocidal people” to different parts of Belgrade. The resolution explicitly states that criminal accountability for genocide is a responsibility that weighs on certain individuals; the “collective guilt” framing was instead manufactured, in the lobbying campaign that preceded the vote, by Vučić and Milorad Dodik (leader of Republika Srpska) themselves. After the UN vote backed the resolution, Vučić, as if the chief doppelgänger of a parallel reality, announced a moral victory based on the sixty-eight abstentions, and he continued campaigning in ongoing local elections. The myth, deployed as a technology of staying in power, always intensifies when there are problems, elections, or challengers to power. The historical arc, the narrative, the explanatory frame was set long ago and is state sponsored at all times, in war and peace alike. Regime members are an integral part of it, either as real characters in concrete historical events, as with Vučić, who served as minister of information during the last phase of Milošević’s rule, or as political actors who benefit materially and politically from keeping the myth alive. To stay in power, it was crucial not to let citizens question their newly found capitalist “paradise” but to keep everybody hostage in this imagined community of war crimes and war thugs; complicit through membership in the same ethnic community, complicit through widespread feelings of loss, guilt, and shame that are being worked out through ethnic drama while covering up mass economic and social losses. Students Win, but With Baggage There were also those who challenged the destructive myth. But they, too, sometimes fell into a collective-guilt framing, screaming nationalism where they could have screamed class. In a rather bizarre string of historical permutations, the German model of postwar reckoning with Nazism, Vergangenheitsbewältigung , or “dealing with the past,” was adopted in the local nongovernmental organization (NGO) lexicon and practice. The concept sat well with the tradition of political liberalism in Serbia, while neglecting the economic workings of the breakup of Yugoslavia and dismissing local histories as possible sources of peace and justice. Still, as Marković points out: We would be completely in the dark related to war crimes if it wasn’t for them. It is also true that war crimes concealed the economic crime called privatization and the disenfranchisement of the broad masses of the people. People close to those in power easily got their hands on those former factories for very little money and cemented their wealth. And now, there’s practically nothing we can do about them. Ingenious tricksters on the political right spotted the weaknesses of the model and invented the charge of auto-chauvinism (the self-hating Serb), which played well on the divide between the urban-educated, culturally snobbish on one side and the rest of the country on the other. This is how the narrative and explanatory framework became squared and closed from all sides. The charge of auto-chauvinism, while never in mass usage, has been repeatedly deployed against the current student movement, transformed into clickbait: students have been called “Ustaše” (supporters of the Nazi-collaborationist regime in Croatia during World War II) and accused of being part of a “color revolution” and of working against Serbs and Serbia. The student-led mass social movement in Serbia began at the end of 2024, sparked by the collapse of a railway station canopy in second city Novi Sad. The students and their electoral list, which will not feature students but their supporters from different sectors and walks of life, are the main challengers to Vučić’s power and the biggest to date. The country, or at least its rebellious part, keeps pushing for political reforms and what is perceived as a never-finished democratization. The socioeconomic agenda, once again, does not feature prominently, although there have been certain changes compared with previous protest mobilizations . Students kept silent about Mladić. Supporters are somewhat understanding, with hopes that a change of government will open up the possibility for these issues to be discussed anew. And there are different approaches and alternative histories to the one in which Mladić, the defender of Serbs, is the central character. There are the many people who crossed identitarian and ethnic lines to help those on the other side. Some died while doing so, killed by people of their own ethnic group. Others resisted, to their own detriment, interethnic pressure and involvement in crimes. There are also alternative histories of the breakup that do not fit neatly into the story of primordial ethnic hatred. One day, there will be no murals of Ratko Mladić in Belgrade. Not because of lonely acts of resistance, but because there will be no political force in power interested in keeping that myth alive. But for the Mladić story to fully lose its grip, the larger narrative framework that sustains it also needs to go. We need to explain to ourselves why not enough people understood that a war was a massive project of collective dispossession. And we need to direct the current social movement to take some of that possession back.

articles.title: With Anti-DSA Bill, Congress Is Red-Baiting Like It’s 1955
articles.author: Ben Burgis
articles.content: As summer turns into fall, the United States remains mired in a wildly unpopular war in Iran. On the home front, inflation is stubbornly persistent. All indications point to the president’s party suffering major losses in the November midterms — if, that is, the various Republican attempts to interfere with the integrity of the election fall short.Even with all this going on, though, the House found time on Tuesday to pass a resolution symbolically condemning the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and “all forms of socialism,” quite obviously inspired by Zohran Mamdani’s mayoralty and the primary victories of several DSA-backed congressional candidates.The anti-DSA bill is a strange document. It starts so similarly to the other congressional resolutions condemning socialism over the last two years that I initially wondered whether the authors had simply cut and pasted an earlier one.Whereas socialist ideology necessitates a concentration of power that has, time and time again, collapsed into communist regimes, totalitarian rule, and repressive dictatorships;Whereas socialism has repeatedly led to famine and mass murders, and the killing of over 100,000,000 people worldwide;Then it cuts to up-to-the-minute complaints about DSA and the socialist mayor of New York.Whereas, since the November 2025 New York City mayoral election of a Democratic Socialist, candidates for public office affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have run in over one hundred elections in at least half the states;Whereas the DSA’s ideological tenet labeled “Democracy for All” calls for noncitizens and incarcerated criminals to vote in American elections;Whereas the DSA’s ideological tenet labeled “A Democratic Congress” calls for abolishing the U.S. Senate, implementing ranked choice voting in all elections, and replacing the two-party system;Whereas, on February 19, 2026, the DSA stated “[t]he United States of America has never been a democracy”;Whereas the DSA’s ideology and socialism, in any form, are incompatible with American values and the United States Constitution;In the final “resolved” section, the House “condemns and denounces socialism in all its forms, including the Democratic Socialists of America, and opposes the implementation of socialist policies in the United States.” But between here and there are hundreds of words of phantasmagoric Trumpian fearmongering about noncitizens illegally registering to vote in American elections. The only tenuous connection is that DSA’s platform calls for changing the laws so that everyone who lives in the United States is allowed to vote. But it reads as if whoever drafted the resolution had a particularly hysterical Fox News segment about noncitizen voting playing in the background, got distracted, and switched topics halfway through.The resolution’s nominal argument is a mess. The first two “whereas” clauses are claims about the crimes of Stalinist regimes. But democratic socialists have always been critical of such regimes, even then. Condemning democratic socialists with claims about the crimes of Stalinist authoritarianism makes about as much sense as an atheist bringing up the Spanish Inquisition to condemn the Southern Baptists.Even rhetorically, the resolution’s strategy of lumping democratic socialists with authoritarian states is dramatically undercut by clauses about DSA’s calls to expand voting rights, abolish the Senate, and enact ranked-choice voting to make it easier for third parties to compete. Letting more people vote, making political representation proportional to the number of voters in each state, and expanding the options on Americans’ ballots would take us much further from anything resembling an authoritarian one-party state.So too little democracy or too much — which is it? One suspects that the latter is the more frightening option for signatories.Playing up crimes committed by Stalinist dictators (whether real ones, Cold War exaggerations, or some messy mixture of the two) is a time-tested way of making socialism sound scary. But ironically, the fearmongering gestures here at the notion that America needs a powerful right-wing authoritarian government to protect us from the socialist menace, which seeks to introduce more democracy at the nation’s peril. Why else would a resolution condemning “all forms of socialism” include hundreds of words on the alleged plague of noncitizen voting and the importance of making it harder to vote?The good news is that the propaganda doesn’t seem to be working on Americans. Far from rallying behind President Donald Trump as an American Julius Caesar who will save the republic from itself by taking on authoritarian powers, the public has made him historically unpopular. Far from DSA being exiled to the margins of American politics, a recent Pew poll found that Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents are far likelier to like leaders who identify as democratic socialists (32 percent) than to dislike them (11 percent). And centrist Democrats in Congress were leery enough of alienating their own constituents that only eight House Democrats joined the 212 House Republicans in voting for it.The Republican-dominated Congress thinks that the mention of the S-word will inspire terror in the hearts of patriotic Americans, as though this were 1955. But it’s wrong to assume the American people are on board.

articles.title: The Rise of the Billionaire Lobby
articles.author: Ben Case
articles.content: You’ve heard of the oil lobby, the tobacco lobby, the Israel lobby, the charter school lobby. Behind all of these are billionaires who benefit from the underlying industries or sectors, and whose corporations use their resources to lobby the government for favorable policies. Now, in reaction to a California ballot initiative for the world’s first billionaire tax, we have an innovation: a lobby for billionaires themselves. Self-advocacy by wealthy people is nothing new, of course. But faced with the prospect of persuading voters to reject Proposition 40 — a temporary tax on roughly two hundred unfathomably rich individuals to fund health care for millions of people — billionaires must make the case to the public that forcing them to share a small amount of their fortunes would do more harm than good. At a time when half of American families can’t afford basic necessities, and 95 percent of the country understands that we’re in an affordability crisis, that’s going to be a tough sell. A handful of billionaires led by Google cofounder Sergey Brin are out to prove that money can buy anything. They are pouring unprecedented resources into a political campaign to convince — or if that doesn’t work, to trick — California voters into prioritizing billionaires’ wealth over their own livelihoods. When Billionaires Don’t Get Their Way In October 2025, a labor union of California hospital and health care workers announced their intention to qualify a billionaire tax initiative for the state ballot. Written in collaboration with leading progressive economists like Emmanuel Saez and Robert Reich , it would levy a onetime 5 percent tax on the net assets of billionaires residing in California as of January 1, 2026. The tax would raise $100 billion in one shot, $90 billion of which would be used to fund Medi-Cal, the state’s Medicaid program, which is otherwise facing a dire fiscal cliff thanks to Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill. The remaining $10 billion would go into public education. By December, before the campaign was even circulating petitions, billionaires like Peter Thiel, Sergey Brin, and Larry Page were rushing to move assets out of state. Whether or not they’d end up avoiding the tax (or actually stop spending time and money in California), they’d jump-start the narrative that taxing billionaires would chase them away — a story the billionaire lobby would lean heavily on. A small cohort of billionaires began organizing to undermine the billionaire tax and keep it from reaching voters. They flooded the market for paid signature-gatherers (which all large initiative campaigns use even if volunteers do the bulk of the work) and allegedly even attempted to buy out a key canvassing firm. These efforts multiplied costs for the billionaire tax campaign, while the glut of clipboard-wielding canvassers on the streets made the job of billionaire tax volunteers significantly more difficult. The billionaires also enlisted the help of Governor Gavin Newsom. Shortly after chatting with Brin about the matter at a crypto mogul’s holiday party, Newsom took a stand against the billionaire tax, vowing he’d defeat the campaign one way or another. Following the lead of Newsom and billionaire donors, a handful of liberal nonprofits and labor unions came out against the billionaire tax as well, joining forces with Republicans and business groups to defeat it — all without an alternative plan to fund Medi-Cal once Trump’s cuts kick in next year. So far, all these efforts have come to naught. The billionaire tax qualified by submitting over 1.6 million signatures, more than double the required number, becoming Proposition 40 on November’s ballot. It’s since been endorsed by the California Federation of Labor Unions and a host of other labor groups, the California Nurses Association, and recently the state Democratic Party. Now Brin and his billionaires must convince a majority of voters that closing hospitals, clinics, and emergency rooms is preferable to taxing billionaires who won’t miss the money. Behold a Billionaire Lobby Brin’s anti–Proposition 40 organization is called Building a Better California. It’s the kind of innocuous and unmemorable name given to so many political nonprofits, in this case also seeming to hint at Joe Biden’s bygone Build Back Better infrastructure bill, perhaps to remind us of the billionaire lobby’s bipartisan nature. Building a Better California has already raised more than $150 million, most of it from Brin himself. The group recently dropped its first major advertisement buy, a working-class-centered commercial that also highlights Newsom’s opposition to Prop 40. The ad mentions neither the billionaires themselves nor the fact that Newsom is a longtime personal friend of Brin’s. Brin’s group is expected to spend upward of $90 million on ads, an airtime spending advantage eleven thousand times that of Prop 40’s current budget. The group has already blanketed the terrain with mailers, sending colorful foldouts to every California household warning that the billionaire tax will destroy the state. The purpose, it seems, is to spread confusion and misinformation, and most of all to divert attention from the jaw-dropping profits billionaires have been raking in as day-to-day life gets harder for most Americans. Brin alone, who theoretically would owe something like $9 billion should Prop 40 pass, grew his net wealth by around $100 billion in the past year alone . Billionaires do themselves few favors when they pull back the curtain, giving the public a glimpse of their personalities and priorities. Take, for example, Peter Thiel’s obsession with the Antichrist and Elon Musk’s “transhumanist” desire to implant AI in your brain. Consequently, rather than appealing to the public outright, they know it’s smarter to throw the public off the scent, which is Building a Better California’s raison d’être . The most rational argument against a billionaire tax is that the superrich will relocate to other states, as Thiel, Brin, and Page claim to have done (though some argue the moves were only on paper), depriving California of both the jobs and the taxes these individuals supposedly supply. But this idea has been roundly debunked, from academic studies to recent examples like the 2022 Massachusetts millionaire’s tax, after which the number of millionaires in the Bay State actually increased , with the tax generating billions more in revenue than anticipated. The fact that the billionaire flight argument is still rolled out makes it clear that it is not an evidence-based statement but a threat, albeit a relatively empty one. Texas billionaire Mark Cuban voiced this directly when he said he’d refuse to invest in any California company if Prop 40 passes. The billionaires are essentially saying to the public: “You can’t tax us, otherwise we’ll leave, and then you won’t be able to tax us.” The inherent flimsiness of this argument enhances the need to keep fearmongering , sans credible evidence or details, that the tax will collapse the economy. Evasions abound. Interviewed about Prop 40 on California Insider , Stanford economics professor Joshua Rauh began with the capital flight argument, but before long his commentary took a revealing turn. “There is a principle here of protecting private property,” he said. “It’s a very slippery slope, because who is actually wealthy?” The question was asked with an air of Socratic profundity, even though Prop 40 very clearly defines the taxable group as individuals who own more than $1 billion in assets. “From a philosophical standpoint,” Rauh went on, “would you want the same treatment as what we’re doing to billionaires?” The billionaire lobby needs to convince voters to identify with them — despite the fact that, aside from cellular-level processes like the Krebs cycle, a working person has nothing in common with a tech oligarch worth $258 billion. But Rauh came dangerously close to saying the quiet part out loud. The very point of redistributive proposals like the billionaire tax is that everyone else wants some of the same treatment given to billionaires. Most people pay a much higher real percentage of taxes than billionaires do and yet still struggle to get by. Most people can’t afford to pursue their dreams and passions like billionaires can. And politicians don’t prioritize most people’s needs the way they do billionaires’. Perhaps anticipating their persuasion falling short with the public, even with the money they’re planning to burn on it, the billionaire lobby has a backup plan. Brin personally donated over $100 million to qualify two poison pill initiatives, Propositions 41 and 42, which at a glance appear unrelated to Prop 40 but would nullify the billionaire tax if passed with a higher vote count. To the billionaire class, voters are nuisances to be interfaced with only when strictly necessary. If an unwanted issue can be kept off the ballot, all the better. If not, try to convince people it will spell destruction. Failing that, simply trick them into voting contrary to their own wishes. A Mask-Off Moment For the Superrich The billionaire lobby as it’s being constructed in California is a reaction to Proposition 40, but it’s also reflective of a moment when there are more billionaires in and around the White House than ever before. Billionaires have grown their personal wealth by orders of magnitude as daily life grinds down just about everyone else. The recent acceleration is part of a half-century-long class war offensive in which nearly $80 trillion has been siphoned from the working and middle classes to the superrich. The California billionaire tax is an attempt to protect health care for millions and health care sector jobs for hundreds of thousands. It also says, in clear and concrete terms, that billionaires have taken too much, and that it’s time to use some of that wealth for the public good. And because it is being put up for a majority vote as a ballot initiative, the billionaires are being forced to have a public conversation about their wealth. The billionaire lobby’s purpose, then, is not only to defeat Prop 40 but to justify billionaires’ existence and their place as society’s ultimate decision-makers.
